1.pericope_label: Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus, unto the church of the Thessalonians which is in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. We give thanks to God always for you all, making mention of you in our prayers; Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father;

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin both read the opening as a lesson in unearned standing. Gill canvasses the conjectured reasons for the missing apostolic title without settling on one, and on the thanksgiving presses that it covers every member without distinction and ascribes nothing to free will, previous dispositions, or diligence — nor anything to Paul and his companions, who were only ministers by whom they believed. He also takes the remembering of verse 3 as the reason for the mention in prayer rather than a second act alongside it. Calvin makes the bare name evidence that the Thessalonians acknowledged Paul voluntarily, since he claims the title elsewhere only where authority is contested, and turns the praise of their graces into a spur: recognising the gifts as God’s humbles a pious mind, where confidence in supposed virtues of one’s own makes it careless.

Henry accounts for the missing title by the absence of any challenge — the apostleship was neither doubted at Thessalonica nor opposed there — and reads the joining of Silvanus and Timotheus as humility and as an honour deliberately put upon ministers of inferior rank. On verse 2 he makes thanksgiving itself the duty under discussion: it belongs to God as the author of all good done to us or by us, is to be performed constantly, and is owed not only for the favours we ourselves receive but for benefits bestowed on others.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the setting and the grammar. Barnes places Thessalonica as the seaport of Macedonia at the head of the Thermaic gulf, and infers from the mention of prayer both that Paul prayed constantly and that he prayed extemporaneously, since fixed forms could not have been adapted to churches still being organised. Ellicott holds that a church so familiar needed no reminder of the apostleship, notes the same omission in Philippians and Philemon, and rejects both the early-date and the courtesy explanations as disproved by 1 Thessalonians 2:6; he gives Silas precedence as the man of higher standing, glosses “always” as on every occasion that reminds us of you, and reads the three genitives as emphatic adjectives governed throughout by “in our Lord.” Robertson treats the opening as a nominative absolute in customary letter form, identifies Silvanus as a Jew and Roman citizen and Timothy as the son of a Jewish mother and Greek father while denying either any share in authorship, and observes that the plural implies all three prayed together.

Clarke and Wesley both read verse 3 as a graded description of an active piety. Clarke adds the civic history — the city named by Philip of Macedon for his victory over the Thessalians, or from Cassander’s wife, and taken from the Venetians by the Turks in 1431 — then distinguishes a faith that is operative rather than speculative, a love that labours because it can do more than faith does, and a hope willing to endure hardship where God is most honoured by the endurance. Wesley compresses the same reading into a formula, that faith works, love labours, and hope patiently suffers all things, and draws the inference that those who do not thus labour do not love.

Chrysostom asks the narrow question why Timothy is joined to the salutation here when he is not in the letter to Ephesus, and answers from Paul’s travel plans: he was about to send Timothy to them, so writing about him was superfluous.

Tertullian does not comment on the salutation at all. His block, taken from an argument against an apostle of a rival god, opens by saying the shorter epistles repay attention because brief works carry much pungency, and then runs straight past chapter 1 into the body of the letter: it expounds ‘who both killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets’ at 1 Thessalonians 2:15, arguing that the crimes form a climax and so must have been committed against one and the same Lord, and it goes on to the sanctification of 1 Thessalonians 4:3. The material is genuinely Tertullian on this epistle, but it is stamped at the wrong verse.

debates: Whether the missing apostolic title means anything. Gill leaves the reasons at the level of conjecture; Henry and Ellicott agree it reflects an unchallenged standing; Calvin makes it positive evidence of the readers’ voluntary submission. Ellicott alone names and rejects two further readings — that the omission marks an early date, or a courtesy to Silvanus and Timothy — as disproved by 1 Thessalonians 2:6.

How much weight the plural “we” carries. Robertson takes it to mean the three missionaries prayed together; Ellicott holds that all three are regarded as writers and their sentiments expressed, while the letter remains Paul’s own composition, and Robertson denies the companions any authorial share outright.

What “always” means in verse 2. Ellicott expressly denies it is equivalent to “without ceasing” and limits it to every occasion that recalls them; Robertson keeps a constant attitude of prayer while conceding the prayer was not always audible.
outliers: Barnes answers the opening chiefly with topography and civil history rather than with the salutation’s wording, giving a long account of the city and its situation before reaching the text.
themes: salutation without apostolic title
Silvanus and Timothy joined to Paul
thanksgiving for the whole church
grace as against free will and desert
faith, love and hope as the abiding triad
work, labour and patient endurance
constant and extemporary prayer
Thessalonica and its setting

4.pericope_label: Knowing, brethren beloved, your election of God. For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance; as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake. And ye became followers of us, and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Ghost: So that ye were ensamples to all that believe in Macedonia and Achaia.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin read the passage as a chain running from an eternal decree to its visible evidence. Gill defines the election as the Father’s choice of persons in Christ before the world began, expressly excluding election to office, election to the outward Gospel, and effectual calling — the last because verse 5 presents it as this election’s fruit. He guards “our gospel” against misreading (entrusted to the preachers, not authored by them or about them) and sets it against the false teachers’ message, limits the following of verse 6 to that in the apostles which followed Christ, and notes the Alexandrian reading “of God” alongside “of Christ.” Calvin makes God’s honouring of Paul’s ministry the means by which their adoption was manifested to them, takes the agreement between preaching and faith as itself an attestation of election since God both begins salvation by calling and perfects it by fashioning hearts to obedience, and counts it a great thing to have outstripped believers who began the course earlier.

Henry treats verse 6 as the evidence of the apostles’ success. He stresses that Paul demeaned himself well not merely for his own credit but for others’ benefit, so that his preaching and his living were all of a piece and he did not pull down with one hand what he built with the other; the Thessalonians, having observed what manner of men the preachers were among them, showed a conscientious care to imitate that example.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the text-critical and structural work. Barnes reports the marginal pointing “beloved of God, your election” without thinking the sense materially altered, refers the knowing to Paul, Silas and Timothy, maps the argument as reception (verses 5–7) followed by propagation (verses 8–10), denies that imitation made the preachers heads of a sect, and derives “ensample” from the mark left by a blow through die to model. Ellicott holds the Greek idiom forbids the Authorised rendering of verse 4 outright, limits election to a gracious admission into present religious privileges implying nothing about a final condition, argues from “as ye know” that the power and assurance are the preachers’ and not the converts’, itemises three imitated points, prefers the singular “ensample” so that the whole church is the model, and notes that Macedonia and Achaia comprised all Roman Greece. Robertson leaves the particle in verse 5 undecided among three senses, weighs the manuscripts for singular against plural in verse 7, and observes how daring it is to ask imitation of a preacher, safeguarded only by the added “and of the Lord.”

Clarke and Wesley both resist a decretal reading and both locate the proof in felt power. Clarke restricts the election the Thessalonians knew to the calling of the Gentiles into privileges the Jews had rejected, and states flatly that no irrespective, unconditional, eternal and personal election to everlasting glory is meant; the power of verse 5 he takes as miraculous manifestation to eye and heart, urging a changed heart and life rather than any religious institution, and he holds the consolations of believing more than counterbalanced the persecutions. Wesley grounds the knowledge of election in faith and plain proofs, and reads verse 5 experientially: conviction of sin and need of a Saviour, outward testimony by miracles and by the Spirit’s descent through laying on of hands, and full assurance as the love of God is shed abroad in the heart.

Chrysostom enters only at second hand, as the authority Calvin follows on the participle of verse 4: he understands the knowing of Paul and his colleagues rather than of the Thessalonians, and Calvin adopts that reading against the one Erasmus gave.

debates: What “election” denotes. Gill makes it the eternal choice of individuals to everlasting life and rules out three weaker senses; Clarke expressly denies that any unconditional personal election to glory is in view, confining it to the calling of the Gentiles; Ellicott independently limits it to admission into present religious privileges, implying nothing about a final condition. Wesley makes it knowable through faith and proofs without defining its object.

Whose “knowing” verse 4 reports. Barnes assigns it to Paul, Silas and Timothy; Calvin notes that Erasmus referred it to the Thessalonians instead, and follows Chrysostom in taking it of the preachers as a fuller confirmation of what precedes.

Whether the Authorised pointing of verse 4 is admissible. Barnes records the alternative and judges the sense not materially varied; Ellicott holds that the Greek idiom cannot allow the Authorised rendering.

Whose power and assurance verse 5 describes. Clarke and Wesley describe effects produced in the hearers; Ellicott argues from the following clause “as ye know” that the power, assurance and Holy Ghost are the preachers’ own.
outliers: Robertson raises a caution none of the others voice, that expecting people to imitate a preacher is a daring thing and perilous because imitation fastens readily on the wrong features; he treats “and of the Lord” as the clause that makes the demand safe.
themes: election and its evidences
eternal decree against present privilege
the gospel not in word only
power, Holy Ghost and full assurance
imitation of preachers and of Christ
joy in the midst of affliction
the church as a model to others
Macedonia and Achaia

8.pericope_label: For from you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad; so that we need not to speak any thing. For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God; And to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, even Jesus, which delivered us from the wrath to come.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin both read the passage from the object of faith outward. Gill hears a trumpet in “sounded out” and distinguishes three senses in which the message is the Lord’s — from him as author, of him as subject, by him as dispenser — concluding it is to be received not as the word of man; he takes the reporters of verse 9 to be those to whom the news was brought, and expounds the waiting by the eternal Sonship of one who was incarnate, obeyed, suffered, died, rose and ascended, and will descend to judge the world in righteousness. Calvin calls the sounding forth an elegant metaphor for a faith so lively that it roused other nations and left Paul nothing to publish, finds verse 9 stating in order man’s condition before the gospel, the end for which God instructs us, and the gospel’s fruit, and grounds the waiting on Christ’s resurrection, since minds give way at every turn unless they look to him and he rose so that his members might share his glory.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson work the language and the claim. Barnes develops the trumpet into an echo among the hills and vales of Greece and argues the diffusion was at first involuntary, a necessary result of conversion rather than a plan; he treats the report of verse 9 as testimony to the preachers’ own conduct and disinterest, and holds the second coming was prominent in the Thessalonian preaching without inferring it was pressed there more than elsewhere. Ellicott corrects “rang” to “has rung,” observes the clauses are not quite logically balanced, glosses “your faith” as the report of it rather than a creed, identifies the reporters as the inhabitants of those countries telling the preachers their own story, and makes the two infinitives of verse 10 describe the condition turning produced rather than its intention — then shifts both tenses, reading “delivereth” and a wrath already on its way from which Christ saves day by day. Robertson notes the verb for sounding forth occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, likens the church to a sounding board or transmitting station, allows a pardonable touch of hyperbole, marks the reporting as voluntary and continuous, and takes the waiting as linear, a hope real and powerful with Paul yet open to abuse then as now.

Clarke and Wesley both explain the spread by ordinary means and both weigh the deliverance carefully. Wesley notes Thessalonica’s great commerce, treats the report as echoed from them, and divides the deliverance into three — redeemed once, delivered continually, and delivered at last from the eternal vengeance — while taking the resurrection as proof of the coming judgment. Clarke adds that the city’s situation for traffic carried the news through Macedonia, Achaia and Greece, and that the converts’ conduct left friends able to speak without a blush and adversaries with nothing to allege; he infers from the turning from idols that the majority of the church were heathen Greeks rather than Jews or devout persons, expounds “living” against stocks and stones and “true” against a system false in objects, pretensions, promises and prospects, and gives the wrath a historical as well as a penal reference.

Chrysostom approaches verse 8 by simile rather than by philology. Sweet-smelling ointment does not keep its fragrance shut up in itself but diffuses it abroad and conveys it to the senses of those nearby; so men of conspicuous virtue do not shut their virtue within themselves but benefit many by their good report and make them better. He applies this directly to the Thessalonians, who filled their neighbours with instruction.

debates: What “the wrath to come” is and when it arrives. Ellicott reads the participle as present — a wrath already on its way, with Christ delivering day by day — and prefers “delivereth” to the past tense. Wesley keeps all three moments, a completed redemption, a continuing deliverance, and a future rescue from eternal vengeance. Clarke alone attaches a historical referent, the destruction about to fall on the unbelieving and impenitent Jews, alongside the punishment due for sin.

How literally the spread of the report should be taken. Calvin takes the claim at face value, that the news had gone far enough that Paul need not publish it; Robertson grants a pardonable touch of hyperbole; Clarke and Wesley supply a natural mechanism in the city’s trade rather than treating the diffusion as extraordinary.

Who “they themselves” are in verse 9. Gill takes them to be those who received the reports; Ellicott the inhabitants of the countries named; Robertson specifically the men of Macedonia, and adds that they report voluntarily and continuously.

What the infinitives of verse 10 express. Ellicott denies they state the converts’ intention in turning and makes them describe the resulting condition; Robertson reads the waiting as linear without raising the question.
outliers: Chrysostom argues the verse by an image none of the others use — ointment whose fragrance cannot be confined — and draws a general moral about conspicuous virtue benefiting bystanders, where the rest attend to the trumpet metaphor in the text itself.

Barnes uses verse 9 to defend the preachers’ motives, taking the converts’ reputation as evidence that Paul and his companions were not moved by selfish or sinister aims; the others read the verse as being about the Thessalonians.
themes: the word of the Lord sounded forth
faith reported beyond Macedonia and Achaia
turning to God from idols
the living and true God
waiting for the Son from heaven
the resurrection as ground of hope
deliverance from the wrath to come
the church as witness to its preachers
